name: Patan (Lalitpur)
tagline: The Newar city of bronze casters, Buddhist courtyards and fine temples
meta_description: Patan (Lalitpur) guide: Durbar Square, Patan Museum, Golden Temple, bronze workshops, Newari cooking, entry fees, how to reach from Kathmandu and when to go.
summary: Patan, officially Lalitpur, is the Newar city across the Bagmati River from Kathmandu, about 5 km south of Thamel. Its Durbar Square, the Patan Museum, the Golden Temple and more than a hundred Buddhist courtyards make it the valley's best place for art and crafts, and half a day to a full day covers it well.
intro: Patan's Newar name is Yala, and its Sanskrit name, Lalitpur, means city of beauty. It was one of the three Malla kingdoms of the valley until 1768 and has always been the most Buddhist of them, with more than a hundred bahals, the monastery courtyards where Newar Buddhist families live, worship and hold festivals. Patan is also the valley's craft capital. Shakya and Bajracharya families still cast bronze statues here by the lost-wax method, and Patan workshops supply images to monasteries and temples across the Himalaya.

The centre is Durbar Square, a compact plaza of temples facing the old royal palace. Krishna Mandir, a stone shikhara temple completed in 1637, stands at one end, and the palace courtyards hold the Patan Museum and, in Sundari Chowk, the carved royal bath of Tusha Hiti. North of the square are the Golden Temple, or Kwa Bahal, and the five-roof Kumbheshwar temple, while to the south-east the terracotta Mahabouddha temple is covered with small images of the Buddha. All of them lie within a 15-minute walk of each other.

Patan has also become the valley's café and design quarter. Jhamsikhel and Pulchowk, on the north-west side, are full of restaurants, bakeries and craft shops, with UN offices and many NGOs nearby. Jawalakhel has the Tibetan refugee carpet workshops, where you can watch wool spun and knotted by hand. Entry to Durbar Square costs NPR 1,000 for foreigners and NPR 250 for SAARC nationals; check current status before you travel. The weather matches Kathmandu's, with the clearest days from October to December and warm, wet afternoons from June to September.
facts: Krishna Mandir, Patan Museum, bronze casting, Rato Machhindranath festival

highlights.title: Krishna Mandir
highlights.text: King Siddhi Narasimha Malla completed this stone temple in 1637, one of the finest shikhara-style temples in Nepal. Carved friezes on its first and second floors tell the stories of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Non-Hindus may not go inside, but the carving faces outwards, and the square is fullest at Krishna Janmashtami in August or September.

highlights.title: Patan Museum
highlights.text: Set in Keshav Narayan Chowk, a restored palace courtyard, the Patan Museum is widely rated the best museum in Nepal for Hindu and Buddhist sacred art. Its galleries explain bronze casting, iconography and temple building in clear English, and the garden café at the back makes a good lunch stop.

highlights.title: Golden Temple (Kwa Bahal)
highlights.text: A short walk north of Durbar Square, this Buddhist monastery founded in the 12th century has a gilded three-roof shrine, a courtyard crowded with bronze figures and a few resident turtles. A boy under 12 serves as temple priest for a month at a time. Remove shoes and leather at the door and pay a small entry fee.

highlights.title: Kumbheshwar temple
highlights.text: One of only two free-standing five-roof pagodas in the valley, Kumbheshwar was first built in 1392 and is dedicated to Shiva. Its spring-fed pond is said to be connected to Gosaikunda lake, and on Janai Purnima in August thousands come to bathe and renew their sacred threads.

highlights.title: Bronze workshops and Mahabouddha
highlights.text: South-east of the square, the lanes around Mahabouddha are lined with metal workshops where artisans model statues in wax, coat them in clay and pour molten bronze. The terracotta Mahabouddha temple, covered in small Buddha images, stands in a tight courtyard; climb to a neighbouring rooftop shop for the best view of its tower.

highlights.title: Rato Machhindranath chariot festival
highlights.text: Patan's longest festival hauls a towering chariot of the rain god Bunga Dyah through the city in stages over several weeks, usually starting in April or May and ending at Jawalakhel with the showing of the sacred bhoto vest. Dates follow the lunar calendar and can stretch for a month; check current status before you travel.

how_to_reach.text: Patan is about 5 km south of Thamel across the Bagmati, 20–40 minutes by car or taxi depending on traffic at the Thapathali and Kupondole bridges. Taxis and ride-hailing cars cost roughly NPR 400–700; check current rates. Our day tours usually drop you at Mangal Bazaar, at the south-east corner of Durbar Square, and collect you there or at Pulchowk.

Tribhuvan International Airport is about 8 km away, a 25–45 minute drive. Guests with an afternoon departure can fit Patan Durbar Square and the museum into the morning, and Patan is a calm base for a first or last night close to the airport.

From central Kathmandu you can walk to Patan in about an hour via the Thapathali bridge and Kupondole, though traffic makes it more pleasant as a one-way walk. Inside Patan everything is on foot: Durbar Square, the Golden Temple, Kumbheshwar and Mahabouddha all lie within about 1 km of each other.

where_to_stay: Most of our guests visit Patan from a Kathmandu hotel, but staying here gives a quieter base. Inside the old town, a few small guesthouses and boutique stays in restored Newar houses sit within five minutes of Durbar Square, with rooftop views of the temples and early-morning access before visitors arrive. Kupondole, on the rise above the Bagmati, has several long-running mid-range hotels looking back across Kathmandu. Jhamsikhel and Pulchowk suit longer stays and families, with quiet residential streets, cafés and supermarkets, and both are 10–20 minutes by taxi from Durbar Square.
tips: Keep your Durbar Square ticket with you, since staff check it at several approaches to the square and the palace courtyards.
When buying a bronze statue, ask whether it was cast in one piece or several and whether it is fire-gilded or electroplated, because that explains most of the price difference.
Remove shoes and any leather belts or bags before entering the Golden Temple and other Buddhist courtyards that ask for it.
Rooftop cafés around Durbar Square give the best view of the temples in late-afternoon light, so order a tea and stay for sunset.
Allow extra time on Saturdays, the weekly holiday, when Nepali families visit the square and the museum fills up.

experiences.title: Patan Museum and Durbar Square visit
experiences.summary: A guided half day in Patan's royal square: the stone Krishna Mandir, the palace courtyards with the royal bath of Tusha Hiti, and about two hours in the Patan Museum, where galleries of bronzes and woodcarving explain the art you will see on every temple in the valley.
body: We start at Mangal Bazaar around 9 am and work north through Durbar Square. Your guide shows you the octagonal stone Chyasin Dewal, the Bhimsen temple with its gilded balcony, the Vishwanath temple guarded by stone elephants and the pillar of King Yoganarendra Malla, who kneels facing the palace under a cobra hood with a small bird perched on top. Local legend says that while the bird remains, the king may yet return. Then we stand before Krishna Mandir to read its carved friezes of the Mahabharata and Ramayana from outside.

The palace has three main courtyards. Mul Chowk, the largest and oldest, was the setting for royal ceremonies and is flanked by the Taleju temples. Sundari Chowk holds Tusha Hiti, a sunken royal bath lined with stone carvings of gods and serpents that was restored after the 2015 earthquake. Access to individual courtyards varies with restoration work, so we confirm on the day. Keshav Narayan Chowk, the northern courtyard, houses the Patan Museum, restored with Austrian help and opened in 1997.

Inside the museum we spend about two hours. Galleries cover Hindu and Buddhist iconography, the lost-wax casting process with tools and moulds from Patan workshops, and the structure of a pagoda temple from foundation to pinnacle. Labels are in clear English, and once you have seen these ideas explained, every temple you visit afterwards is easier to read. Foreigners pay NPR 1,000 and SAARC nationals NPR 250 for the square; museum entry arrangements change, so check current status before you travel. Lunch in the garden café behind the museum rounds off the morning.

faqs.q: Is the Patan Museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the best introduction to Nepali sacred art you will find. In about two hours its galleries of bronze, stone and wood sculpture and its lost-wax casting display explain what you see on temples across the valley. It occupies a restored palace courtyard, and its clear English labels make it especially useful for first-time visitors.

faqs.q: What are Patan Durbar Square opening hours?
faqs.a: The square is a public space you can walk through at any hour, and the ticket booths staff the approaches through daylight hours. The Patan Museum keeps shorter hours, usually from mid-morning to late afternoon, and can close on some public holidays. Times change, so check current status before you travel and aim to arrive by 10 am.

faqs.q: Do Indians pay the foreigner rate at Patan Durbar Square?
faqs.a: No. Indian nationals pay the SAARC rate, which has been NPR 250 (about ₹160) against NPR 1,000 for other foreigners, and Nepali citizens enter free. Carry a passport or voter ID to show at the ticket booth if asked. Fees change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Golden Temple and Patan bahal courtyards walk
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹1,800 per person plus small temple fees
experiences.summary: A slow two-and-a-half-hour walk through Patan's Buddhist courtyards, from the gilded Golden Temple to Kumbheshwar's five-roof pagoda, the terracotta Mahabouddha and smaller bahals where Newar families still live around their shrines, with a guide who explains how the courtyards work.
body: Patan has more than a hundred bahals and bahils, the courtyards of Newar Buddhist monasteries. Most were founded as monasteries centuries ago and later filled with the families of their hereditary priests, the Shakyas and Bajracharyas, who still live around the central shrine. From the street, the entrance is often just a low doorway between shops. Step through and you find a paved square with a chaitya, prayer wheels, children playing and someone drying clothes on a balcony carved two hundred years ago.

The walk begins at Kwa Bahal, the Golden Temple, a few minutes north of Durbar Square. Its gilded three-roof shrine, monkey and elephant figures and the turtles that wander the courtyard make it the most elaborate bahal in Patan, and a boy under 12 serves as its priest for a month at a time. From there we continue to Kumbheshwar, the five-roof Shiva pagoda first built in 1392, before crossing back south past the square to Uku Bahal, with its metal lions, griffins and elephants. Remove shoes and leather before the inner shrines.

The last stop is Mahabouddha, the temple of a thousand Buddhas, built of terracotta tiles each moulded with a Buddha image and squeezed into a courtyard so tight that the best view is from a rooftop next door. On the way, metal workshops let you watch artisans chasing fine detail into newly cast bronze. The route covers about 2.5 km of mostly flat lanes and ends near Durbar Square. Small entry fees or donations apply at some temples; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is a bahal in Patan?
faqs.a: A bahal is the courtyard of a Newar Buddhist monastery, built around a central shrine. Most were founded as monasteries and are now home to families descended from their priests, who still perform daily worship. Patan has more than a hundred of them, from the gilded Golden Temple to quiet residential squares with a single stupa.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists visit the Golden Temple in Patan?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are welcome in the Golden Temple courtyard after paying a small entry fee. Take off your shoes and leave leather belts and bags at the door, walk clockwise, and do not touch the shrine or the boy priest. Photography is generally allowed in the courtyard, but ask before photographing people at worship.

faqs.q: Can I buy a bronze statue in Patan?
faqs.a: Yes. Patan is Nepal's main centre for bronze casting, and many workshops sell straight from the bench. Prices depend on size, detail and finish, and fire-gilded statues cost several times more than plain ones. Ask for a receipt, and get a clearance certificate for antique-looking pieces, because objects over 100 years old cannot legally leave Nepal; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Newari cooking class in a Patan home
experiences.best_time: Late morning or afternoon, all year
experiences.summary: A hands-on class in a Patan family kitchen: shop for vegetables and spices in the local market, then cook and eat a Newar meal of bara, chatamari, aloo tama, achar and momo, with printed recipes to take home and versions for vegetarian and no-onion-garlic diets.
body: Classes take place in the home of a Newar family a short walk from Durbar Square, in a kitchen usually on the top floor, which is traditional in Newar houses where the hearth is kept far from the street. We start with a walk to the vegetable market near Mangal Bazaar to buy greens, radish, tomatoes and spices, and the cook explains Newar staples such as timur, the lemony Sichuan pepper of the hills, mustard oil, fenugreek and jimbu, a dried Himalayan herb used to temper lentils.

Back in the kitchen you cook four or five dishes side by side with the host. Bara, the black-lentil patty, needs the batter ground and whipped to the right lightness. Chatamari, the rice-flour pancake, teaches you to swirl a thin batter on a hot pan. Aloo tama is a sour stew of potato, bamboo shoots and black-eyed beans, and a fresh tomato achar with roasted sesame goes with everything. Folding momos takes the longest, and everyone's first pleats look a little rough.

Then everyone sits down to eat what they have made, usually on low cushions with a brass plate, around 1 pm or 7 pm depending on the session. You get printed recipes and a list of substitutes for ingredients that are hard to find outside Nepal. Classes run for groups of two to eight. We make the menu fully vegetarian on request and can leave out onion and garlic for Jain and some Hindu guests with a day's notice. Allow three and a half hours including the market.

faqs.q: Is the Newari cooking class vegetarian-friendly?
faqs.a: Yes. The core dishes in our class, bara, chatamari, aloo tama, achar and vegetable momo, are all easy to make without meat, and we run fully vegetarian classes on request. With a day's notice the host can also cook without onion and garlic for Jain guests and anyone else who avoids them.

faqs.q: Can children join the Patan cooking class?
faqs.a: Children from about eight can join and usually enjoy folding momos and shaping bara. They need supervision near hot oil and the gas stove, so the host gives them simpler tasks. Child rates apply for under-12s. Tell us their ages when booking so the family can plan the session around them.

faqs.q: Will I be able to cook these dishes at home?
faqs.a: Yes. Every guest gets printed recipes with measurements and a list of substitutes, such as urad dal flour for bara and supermarket rice flour for chatamari. Timur and jimbu are sold in Kathmandu spice shops and keep well in a sealed jar, so most guests buy a small stock before flying home.

faqs.q: Is Patan the same as Lalitpur?
faqs.a: Yes. Patan is the traditional name, Lalitpur the official one, and Yala the name in Newari. Lalitpur Metropolitan City covers the old town and newer districts such as Pulchowk, Jhamsikhel and Jawalakhel. Road signs, buses and hotel addresses use Lalitpur, while travellers and guides usually say Patan for the old city around Durbar Square.

faqs.q: Patan, Bhaktapur or Kathmandu Durbar Square: which should I visit?
faqs.a: If you have time for only one, choose Bhaktapur for atmosphere and Patan for art. Patan's square is the most compact of the three, and the Patan Museum explains Newar art better than anywhere else in Nepal. Kathmandu's square is easiest to reach but busier with traffic. Our three-night Kathmandu city break visits all three.

faqs.q: How much time do I need in Patan?
faqs.a: Half a day covers Durbar Square, the museum and the Golden Temple at a comfortable pace. A full day lets you add Kumbheshwar, Mahabouddha, the bronze workshops and lunch in Jhamsikhel or a cooking class. Many guests combine a morning in Patan with an afternoon in Kirtipur or at the Tibetan carpet workshops in Jawalakhel.

faqs.q: What is the Patan Durbar Square entry fee?
faqs.a: Foreigners pay NPR 1,000 and SAARC nationals NPR 250 to enter Patan Durbar Square, and Nepali citizens enter free. Tickets are sold at booths around the square. Arrangements for the Patan Museum have changed over the years, so ask at the booth what your ticket covers, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get from Thamel to Patan?
faqs.a: The simplest way is a taxi or ride-hailing car, about 20–40 minutes and roughly NPR 400–700 depending on traffic; check current rates. Local microbuses run from the Ratna Park area to Lagankhel and Mangal Bazaar for a fraction of the price. Our guided tours include a private car with pickup from your hotel.

faqs.q: Where can I see Tibetan carpets being made in Patan?
faqs.a: At the Tibetan refugee handicraft centre in Jawalakhel, set up in 1960, and the workshops of the Tibetan settlement around it. You can watch wool being carded, spun, dyed and hand-knotted, and buy carpets with shipping arranged. Jawalakhel is about 2 km south-west of Durbar Square and pairs well with lunch in Jhamsikhel.

faqs.q: Is Patan good for an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a quieter base than Thamel. Patan has small guesthouses in restored Newar houses near Durbar Square and mid-range hotels in Kupondole, with plenty of cafés in Jhamsikhel and Pulchowk. It is 20–40 minutes from Thamel and from the airport, so it works for a first or last night, and families on longer stays often prefer it.

faqs.q: When is the Rato Machhindranath festival in Patan?
faqs.a: The chariot festival of Rato Machhindranath, also called Bunga Dyah Jatra, usually begins in April or May and can run for several weeks as the tall chariot is pulled through Patan in stages. It ends at Jawalakhel with Bhoto Jatra, the public showing of a sacred vest. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Patan on a long layover in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. With at least seven hours between flights and your visa or Indian ID sorted, you can clear immigration, spend three hours at Patan Durbar Square and the museum and return to the airport, which is only about 8 km away. Allow extra time for the evening rush hour and for security at the international terminal.
